domains: Kingship, Strength, Immortality Quest, Walls of Uruk
description_brief: Legendary king of Uruk, two-thirds god and one-third man, who undertakes epic adventures, seeks immortality, and builds Uruk's walls.
notes: Protagonist of the Epic of Gilgamesh. Son of Lugalbanda and Ninsun.

description_brief: Wild man created by Aruru, companion of Gilgamesh in heroic deeds, later dies as divine punishment.
notes: Created by Aruru at Anu's request. Civilized by Shamhat. His death prompts Gilgamish's quest. His spirit appears in Tablet XII.

description_brief: Supreme sky god in the Mesopotamian pantheon, father of Ishtar, involved in divine decisions like the creation of Enkidu and granting the Bull of Heaven.
notes: Member of the primary triad with Enlil and Ea. Resides in E-Anna temple in Uruk.

description_brief: Mother goddess who created Enkidu from clay at Anu's request.
notes: Also known as Belet-ili.

description_brief: God of war and hunting, son of Enlil, mentioned in divine assembly contexts.
notes: Son of Enlil.

description_brief: God of wild animals and cattle, whose domain Enkidu initially shares.
notes: Also known as Shumugan.

description_brief: Sun god and patron deity who aids Gilgamish and Enkidu on their quests.
notes: Patron of travelers and justice. Worshipped by Gilgamish and Enkidu.

domains: Earth, Wind, Storms, Kingship, Divine Authority, Flood
description_brief: Chief god of the pantheon, instigates the Great Flood and decides Enkidu's fate.
notes: Part of the primary triad with Anu and Ea. Often depicted as stern and wrathful.

description_brief: God of wisdom, warns Uta-Napishtim of the flood and facilitates the appearance of Enkidu's spirit.
notes: Part of the primary triad with Anu and Enlil. Also known as Enki and Nin-igi-azag.

description_brief: Gilgamish's mother, a wise goddess who interprets his dreams and seeks divine aid for him.
notes: Described as "all-wise" and "glorious Queen". Implied to be a "cow of the steer-folds" in Tablet II.

description_brief: The immortal man who survived the Great Flood, resides at the edge of the world, and tells Gilgamish his story.
notes: Lives at Dilmun/The Faraway. Son of Ubara-Tutu. Also known as Atra-hasis. Granted immortality by the gods.

description_brief: Divine tavern-keeper at the edge of the world who offers Gilgamish wisdom.
notes: Described as "a goddess who makes wine" or "ale-wife". Her philosophy advocates enjoying life's simple pleasures.

alternate_names: Tutelary god of the House of Gilgamish (epithet)
description_brief: Former king of Uruk and Gilgamish's divine father, invoked for aid and guidance.
notes: Preceded Gilgamish in kings lists. Described as "the god Lugal-banda". Tutelary god of the House of Gilgamish.

description_brief: The ruler of the Underworld, depicted in Enkidu's vision of the realm of the dead.
notes: Wife of Nergal. Also known as Queen of Hades.

description_brief: God of the Underworld and husband of Ereshkigal, involved in allowing Enkidu's spirit to ascend.
notes: Also known as The Croucher. Associated with plague and war.

description_brief: Vizier of the Underworld, a spirit associated with fate and plague.
notes: Also known as Plague-god. Implied as a force of death.

description_brief: Temple courtesan who civilizes Enkidu by introducing him to human society and sexuality.
notes: Initially cursed by Enkidu, later blessed by Shamash. Also known as Hetaera.

description_brief: The mythical ferryman who transports Gilgamish across the lethal Waters of Death.
notes: Also known as Sur-Sunabu in Old Babylonian version. His boat requires poles after Gilgamish destroys its sails.

description_brief: The man who first discovers Enkidu in the wilderness and reports him to Gilgamish.
notes: Also known as Trapper. His actions initiate the meeting between Gilgamish and Enkidu.

description_brief: The formidable monster appointed by Enlil to guard the Cedar Forest, defeated and killed by Gilgamish and Enkidu.
notes: His roar is a whirlwind, flame in his jaws, breath is Death.

description_brief: A monstrous divine bull sent by Ishtar and Anu to punish Gilgamish and Uruk, defeated by Gilgamish and Enkidu.
notes: Sent by Anu at Ishtar's request.

description_brief: Terrifying monstrous beings who guard the entrance to the path of the sun at the mountains of Mashu.
notes: Their glance is Death. Guard the path for Shamash's journey.

description_brief: Storm-god associated with Humbaba's terror and the instigator of the storm during the Great Flood.
notes: Also known as the storm-god. Rumbles within the storm cloud during the flood.

description_brief: Deity mentioned as leading the vanguard of the divine storm forces during the Great Flood.
notes: Mentioned alongside Sharru in Tablet XI.

description_brief: Deity mentioned as leading the vanguard of the divine storm forces during the Great Flood.
notes: Mentioned alongside Nabu in Tablet XI.

description_brief: Divine entity associated with the destructive force of the Great Flood.
notes: Described as wrenching out bollards in Tablet XI.

description_brief: A group of powerful deities forming the divine council, involved in judging fates and decisions like the flood.
notes: Also known as Great gods or Spirits of Heaven. Act as judges in the Underworld.

description_brief: Deity responsible for settling destiny and determining life and death alongside the Anunnaki.
notes: Also known as Maker of Destiny.

description_brief: A group of celestial deities who form the divine council and are upset by the devastation of the Great Flood.
notes: Also known as Gods of heaven. Distinct from the Anunnaki in some traditions.

description_brief: The human boatman to whom Uta-Napishtim entrusts the Ark during the Great Flood.
notes: Mentioned in Tablet XI.

description_brief: A goddess referenced in a traditional mourning lament in Tablet XII.
notes: Also known by the epithet "She who dead lieth" in the lament. Her son is Ninazu, god of healing and the underworld.

description_brief: Deity who serves as the scribe and recorder in the Underworld.
notes: Reads records before Queen Ereshkigal. Mentioned in Enkidu's dream of the Underworld.

description_brief: Legendary hero mentioned as residing in the Underworld in Enkidu's dream.
notes: Hero of his own legend, known for being carried to heaven on an eagle.

description_brief: God of vegetation and husband of Ishtar, mourned annually.
notes: Mentioned by Gilgamish as a former lover of Ishtar. Subject of an annual Wailing festival.

description_brief: A shepherd loved by Ishtar who was transformed into a jackal.
notes: Sacrificed to Ishtar daily. Transformed and driven away by his own herd boy and dogs.

description_brief: The gardener of Ishtar's father, whom she loved and who rejected her, leading her to transform him.
notes: Transformed into a spider-like creature (*dallalu*) after rejecting Ishtar.

description_brief: Goddess of love and war, spurned by Gilgamesh, unleashes the Bull of Heaven upon Uruk. Sometimes identified with the Sumerian goddess Inanna.
The father of Uta-Napishtim.
notes: Mentioned only as Uta-Napishtim's father in the text.

description_brief: The mother of Ishtar and consort of Anu.
notes: Mentioned in Tablet VI when Ishtar complains to her parents after being rejected by Gilgamesh.

description_brief: A god mentioned as a leader or assistant in the divine council planning the Great Flood.
notes: Mentioned by Uta-Napishtim in Tablet XI.

description_brief: Mentioned as the son of 'She who dead lieth' (likely Ereshkigal) in the lament in Tablet XII.
notes: His mother is personified in a lament about the dead.

description_brief: Geatish hero who defeats Grendel and Grendel's mother, later becomes king, and dies fighting the dragon.
notes: Central protagonist whose career links youthful heroic fame to the limits of aged kingship.

description_brief: Danish king whose hall Heorot is ravaged by Grendel until Beowulf comes to aid him.
notes: Functions as elder ruler, patron, and moral counterpoint for Beowulf.

description_brief: Young kinsman who alone remains with Beowulf during the dragon fight.
notes: Embodies comitatus loyalty and inherits the burden of Geatish survival.

description_brief: Danish spokesman who challenges Beowulf and later lends him the sword Hrunting.
notes: His challenge tests heroic reputation before giving way to grudging support.

description_brief: Queen of Hrothgar who serves the hall, speaks diplomatically, and protects her sons' inheritance.
notes: Her speeches reveal the fragile social order behind heroic feasting.

description_brief: King of the Geats and Beowulf's lord and kinsman.
notes: Anchors Beowulf in Geatish dynastic history.

description_brief: Legendary ancestor of the Danish royal line whose ship burial opens the poem.
notes: Frames kingship as both glorious inheritance and mortal passage.

description_brief: Primordial sea mother who becomes the leader of the older gods against Marduk.
notes: Her defeated body becomes the structured cosmos in Enuma Elis.

description_brief: Freshwater abyss and consort of Tiamat, whose plot against younger gods begins the divine conflict.
notes: His death by Ea escalates the conflict that culminates in Marduk's rise.

description_brief: Young god who defeats Tiamat, organizes the cosmos, and receives supreme kingship.
notes: The poem legitimates Babylonian divine and political supremacy through him.

description_brief: Wise god who defeats Apsu and fathers Marduk.
notes: His cunning initiates the younger gods' victory over primordial powers.

description_brief: Sky god and senior divine authority in Mesopotamian myth.
notes: Appears in divine assemblies and transfers power within the pantheon.

description_brief: Tiamat's chosen commander, given the Tablet of Destinies and later killed so humanity can be made from his blood.
notes: His death links defeated rebellion to the creation of human service.

description_brief: Senior primordial god who urges a champion to confront Tiamat.
notes: His inability to solve the crisis prepares Marduk's elevation.

description_brief: One of the Hero Twins who defeats the lords of Xibalba through wit, ordeal, and resurrection.
notes: Paired with Hunahpu as the central culture-hero pair of the Popol Vuh.

description_brief: Hero Twin who journeys to Xibalba and helps defeat the underworld lords.
notes: His death and restoration pattern the Popol Vuh's concern with sacrifice and renewal.

description_brief: Elder creator-grandmother who aids creation and the Hero Twins through counsel and divination.
notes: Represents ancestral knowledge and household continuity.

description_brief: Creator and storm deity involved in forming the world and humanity.
notes: A principal divine voice in the creation sections of the Popol Vuh.

description_brief: Creator deity who participates in the primordial council that forms the world.
notes: Links sovereign authority, watery beginnings, and serpent imagery.

description_brief: Father of the Hero Twins, killed in Xibalba after being summoned to play ball.
notes: His severed head and miraculous conception establish the twins' mission.

description_brief: Ulster champion whose single combats hold back Medb's army during the cattle raid.
notes: His youthful power and tragic isolation dominate the Tain.

description_brief: Queen of Connacht who launches the raid for the Brown Bull of Cooley.
notes: Embodies sovereignty, rivalry, and the economics of prestige.

description_brief: King of Connacht and Medb's husband, whose property contest helps motivate the raid.
notes: Often paired with Medb in scenes of royal calculation.

description_brief: Ulster exile serving Connacht who knows Cú Chulainn and mediates between sides.
notes: His divided loyalties give the raid historical and emotional depth.

description_brief: King of Ulster whose incapacitated warriors leave Cú Chulainn to defend the province.
notes: Represents the polity Cú Chulainn protects.

description_brief: Cú Chulainn's foster brother forced into fatal single combat against him.
notes: His duel is one of the Tain's central tragic episodes.

description_brief: Trojan survivor destined to found the lineage leading to Rome.
notes: The Aeneid makes his private losses serve public foundation.

description_brief: Founder and queen of Carthage whose love for Aeneas ends in death.
notes: Her tragedy gives Rome and Carthage a mythic emotional prehistory.

description_brief: Rutulian leader who opposes Aeneas and fights for Lavinia.
notes: His death closes the epic but leaves Roman destiny morally unsettled.

description_brief: Aeneas' son and dynastic link to the Julian/Roman future.
notes: His presence keeps foundation history visible in family terms.

description_brief: Daughter of Latinus whose marriage to Aeneas becomes the focus of war in Italy.
notes: She is less an agent than the symbolic hinge of Trojan-Latin union.

description_brief: Aeneas' father, carried from Troy and later encountered in the underworld.
notes: He transmits Roman destiny through ancestral vision.

description_brief: Leader of the Argonauts who seeks the Golden Fleece to reclaim royal power.
notes: His success depends heavily on Medea and divine intervention.

description_brief: Daughter of Aeetes whose magic enables Jason to win the Golden Fleece.
notes: A helper in the Argonautica and a dangerous remembered figure in later myth.

description_brief: King of Colchis who sets Jason impossible tasks and guards the Golden Fleece.
notes: Represents the hostile sovereign at the edge of the Greek world.

description_brief: Mythic singer among the Argonauts whose song orders conflict and charms nature.
notes: An archetype for poetic power as ritual technology.

description_brief: Great strongman hero who joins the Argonauts before leaving the expedition.
notes: His presence marks the quest against a wider heroic cycle.

description_brief: Olympian sky king who governs divine order and intervenes across Greek myth.
notes: Central sovereign figure in Greek epic, hymn, and genealogy.

description_brief: Olympian queen associated with marriage, royal status, and opposition to favored rivals.
notes: A major divine actor in the Iliad and Argonautica.

description_brief: Goddess of intelligence, craft, and strategic war who aids heroes such as Odysseus and Diomedes.
notes: Often appears as the divine intelligence behind successful action.

description_brief: God of prophecy, song, plague, healing, and archery.
notes: A major divine agent from Homeric plague to Delphic foundation.

description_brief: Greatest Achaean warrior in the Iliad, torn between glory and early death.
notes: His wrath structures the Iliad's moral and emotional arc.

description_brief: Foremost Trojan defender, husband of Andromache and son of Priam.
notes: His death is the Iliad's deepest image of civic and familial loss.

description_brief: King of Ithaca whose intelligence and endurance drive the Odyssey.
notes: Central model of metis, survival, and contested household restoration.

description_brief: Odysseus' wife who preserves the household through delay, craft, and testing.
notes: Her intelligence mirrors Odysseus' cunning inside domestic space.

description_brief: Son of Odysseus and Penelope who matures while seeking news of his father.
notes: His arc turns household crisis into initiation.

description_brief: Enchantress who transforms Odysseus' men and later advises his journey.
notes: Combines erotic danger, magical power, and eventual guidance.

description_brief: Ancient singer and culture hero whose words and songs shape events in the Kalevala.
notes: The poem repeatedly makes song a form of power through him.

description_brief: Divine smith who forges the Sampo and participates in quests to Pohjola.
notes: Represents technology, craft, and creative labor.

description_brief: Impulsive hero whose adventures include death, dismemberment, and restoration by his mother.
notes: A volatile heroic pattern alongside Väinämöinen and Ilmarinen.

description_brief: Mistress of Pohjola who controls daughters, trials, and the Sampo.
notes: Functions as both sovereign adversary and powerful ritual specialist.

description_brief: Doomed youth whose abuse, vengeance, and accidental incest lead to catastrophe.
notes: The darkest tragic cycle within the Kalevala.

description_brief: High sky and thunder deity invoked for aid, weather, and fertility.
notes: Serves as the poem's chief divine power.

description_brief: Sun goddess whose withdrawal plunges the world into darkness and whose line legitimates imperial descent.
notes: Central deity of the Kojiki's heavenly order.

description_brief: Stormy brother of Amaterasu whose violence causes crisis but who also slays the serpent Yamata no Orochi.
notes: Moves between disruptive trickster and culture hero.

description_brief: Male creator who generates islands and deities with Izanami and later performs purification after visiting the dead.
notes: His purification produces major kami including Amaterasu.

description_brief: Female creator who dies giving birth to fire and becomes associated with Yomi.
notes: Her separation from Izanagi establishes death and pollution boundaries.

description_brief: Earthly deity who wins trials, orders the land, and eventually yields rule to the heavenly line.
notes: A central figure in the negotiation between local and heavenly sovereignty.

description_brief: Imperial prince and warrior whose campaigns extend Yamato power and end in tragic death.
notes: Combines conquest legend with lament for heroic excess.

description_brief: Legendary king whose court organizes many adventures in the Mabinogion.
notes: Functions as a central courtly reference point even when not protagonist.

description_brief: Prince of Dyfed whose exchange with Arawn and marriage to Rhiannon shape the first branch.
notes: His story establishes lawful kingship through restraint and alliance.

description_brief: Otherworld-associated woman who marries Pwyll and suffers wrongful punishment after her child disappears.
notes: Embodies sovereignty, endurance, and contested female agency.

description_brief: Son of Pwyll and Rhiannon, lost in infancy and restored to his lineage.
notes: Links the first four branches through dynastic continuity and rupture.

description_brief: Companion and husband of Rhiannon who endures enchantment and restores order through patience and craft.
notes: A quiet problem-solver rather than a purely martial hero.

description_brief: Inspired bard whose birth and contests display poetic and prophetic power.
notes: A major figure for mythic poetics and metamorphosis.

description_brief: Divine ally and charioteer of Arjuna who teaches the Bhagavad Gita and guides the Pandavas.
notes: Human hero and supreme deity meet in his role.

description_brief: Pandava archer whose hesitation before battle prompts Krishna's teaching.
notes: Central martial and ethical protagonist of the war narrative.

description_brief: Eldest Pandava whose devotion to dharma is tested by exile, war, and rule.
notes: His moral ambiguity makes kingship a field of continual judgment.

description_brief: Kuru elder bound by a terrible vow, warrior on the Kaurava side, and teacher on the bed of arrows.
notes: A central authority figure whose vows both preserve and damage the dynasty.

description_brief: Kaurava prince whose refusal to yield power drives the conflict with the Pandavas.
notes: A complex antagonist tied to entitlement, loyalty, and destructive pride.

description_brief: Great warrior of secret royal birth who remains loyal to Duryodhana.
notes: His life dramatizes generosity, stigma, and tragic allegiance.

description_brief: Shared wife of the Pandavas whose humiliation in the dice hall becomes a moral crisis of the epic.
notes: Her suffering and speech expose failures of kingship and kinship.

description_brief: Prince of Ayodhya and avatar of Vishnu who rescues Sita and restores righteous order.
notes: The Ramayana centers idealized kingship and human cost through him.

description_brief: Rama's wife, abducted by Ravana and repeatedly tested by ordeal and social suspicion.
notes: Her story is central to the epic's tensions around purity and justice.

description_brief: Rama's devoted brother who accompanies him and Sita into exile.
notes: Embodies fraternal loyalty and protective service.

description_brief: Mighty monkey ally who finds Sita and becomes Rama's exemplary devotee.
notes: A key bridge between heroic action and devotional imagination.

description_brief: King of Lanka whose abduction of Sita brings Rama into war.
notes: Powerful and learned, but destroyed by desire and arrogance.

description_brief: Dragon-slaying hero whose strength and hidden vulnerability shape the Nibelungenlied.
notes: His murder unleashes the poem's revenge cycle.

description_brief: Siegfried's widow whose grief becomes catastrophic vengeance.
notes: Her transformation gives the poem its tragic second half.

description_brief: Burgundian retainer who engineers Siegfried's murder and guards the Nibelung treasure.
notes: His loyalty to his lords becomes morally destructive.

description_brief: Burgundian king whose pursuit of Brunhild depends on Siegfried's concealed aid.
notes: His weakness helps set the revenge machinery in motion.

description_brief: Powerful queen won by deception and later drawn into conflict with Kriemhild.
notes: Her injured status exposes the politics of marriage and honor.

description_brief: Chief god associated with wisdom, war, poetry, sacrifice, and the dead.
notes: Central but unstable source of knowledge and doom in Norse myth.

description_brief: Thunder god who defends gods and humans against giants and cosmic threats.
notes: A direct protector figure, often comic and formidable at once.

description_brief: Cunning and dangerous figure whose tricks help and harm the gods and lead toward Ragnarok.
notes: The clearest Norse trickster pattern in the archive.

description_brief: Valkyrie-like heroine whose broken oaths with Sigurd bring ruin.
notes: A central tragic agent in the Volsung-Nibelung cycle.

description_brief: Hero who slays Fafnir, wins cursed treasure, and becomes entangled in tragic oaths.
notes: Norse form of the dragon-slayer cycle.

description_brief: Heroine whose marriages and losses bind the Sigurd and Atli cycles.
notes: Her laments and vengeance carry the emotional center of the heroic poems.

description_brief: God of the dead and resurrected king whose fate structures Egyptian afterlife hope.
notes: Central figure in Pyramid Texts and Book of the Dead.

description_brief: Falcon-associated god and son of Osiris who contests Set and embodies legitimate kingship.
notes: The deceased king is repeatedly identified with Horus and Osiris.

description_brief: Goddess who protects Osiris and Horus through mourning, magic, and maternal power.
notes: A major protective and restorative force in Egyptian mortuary myth.

description_brief: Jackal-associated god of embalming, tomb protection, and rites for the dead.
notes: Guides and protects the deceased through mortuary transition.

description_brief: God of writing, wisdom, and divine record-keeping who appears in judgment scenes.
notes: Makes cosmic and moral order legible through record and measure.

description_brief: Goddess and principle of truth and right order, central to the weighing of the heart.
notes: Connects ethics, cosmos, and afterlife judgment.

description_brief: Powerful god often opposed to Osiris and Horus, associated with disorder and force.
notes: His conflict with Horus structures divine kingship mythology.

description_brief: Vedic warrior god who drinks Soma, releases waters, and defeats Vritra.
notes: The most prominent heroic deity of the Rig Veda.

description_brief: Fire god and sacrificial mediator carrying offerings between humans and gods.
notes: The ritual hinge of many Rig Vedic hymns.

description_brief: Sacred plant/drink and deity pressed in ritual and praised for power and inspiration.
notes: Links material rite, divine agency, and altered state.

description_brief: Sovereign deity associated with rta, oaths, waters, and moral oversight.
notes: A key figure for cosmic and ethical order.

description_brief: Vedic deity paired with Varuna and associated with agreement and social order.
notes: Represents binding relationships within cosmic law.

description_brief: Storm gods who accompany Indra and embody forceful, youthful energy.
notes: A divine troop pattern in the Rig Veda.

description_brief: Dawn goddess praised for bringing light, life, and daily renewal.
notes: Turns cosmic order into a recurring visible event.

description_brief: Great champion of Iran whose victories and sorrows dominate the Shah Nameh selection.
notes: Both defender of kings and tragic father of Sohrab.

description_brief: White-haired hero raised by the Simurgh and father of Rustem.
notes: Links human royal lineage with supernatural nurture.

description_brief: Rustem's son, killed unknowingly by his father in tragic combat.
notes: Central to the archive's father-son recognition tragedy.

description_brief: Serpent-shouldered tyrant whose rule is overthrown by Feridoun.
notes: Embodies corrupt sovereignty and monstrous appetite.

description_brief: Iranian king whose pride and imprudence repeatedly require heroic rescue.
notes: Shows kingship dependent on heroic correction.

description_brief: Righteous Iranian king who avenges wrongs and eventually withdraws from worldly rule.
notes: A model of sacred kingship and renunciation.

description_brief: Primordial Earth mother who births sky, sea, mountains, Titans, and many later powers.
notes: Theogony uses her as a generative foundation and political mover.

description_brief: Primordial Sky and mate of Gaia, overthrown by Kronos after suppressing his children.
notes: His castration marks a decisive succession crisis in cosmic genealogy.

description_brief: Titan ruler who overthrows Ouranos and is himself overthrown by Zeus.
notes: A central figure in Hesiodic succession myth.

description_brief: Mother of the Olympians who hides Zeus from Kronos.
notes: Her deception enables the next cosmic order.

description_brief: Titan who tricks Zeus, shapes sacrificial order, and is punished for aiding humans.
notes: A key figure for culture, suffering, and divine-human tension.

description_brief: Divine singers who authorize Hesiod and preserve genealogical knowledge.
notes: They make poetic memory the foundation of the Theogony.

description_brief: Poet-narrator of the Theogony who receives authority from the Muses.
notes: Important as the archive's named transmitter for the Greek genealogical corpus.

description_brief: Messenger and trickster god whose hymn celebrates theft, negotiation, and invention.
notes: A major figure for boundary crossing and clever speech.

description_brief: Grain goddess whose search for Persephone explains seasonal loss and sacred rites.
notes: Central deity of the longest Homeric Hymn.

description_brief: Daughter of Demeter taken by Hades and made queen of the dead.
notes: Her cyclical absence and return link agriculture with death.

description_brief: Ruler of the underworld who takes Persephone as his bride.
notes: A sovereign figure at the boundary between fertility and death.

description_brief: Goddess of love and desire, powerful over gods and mortals.
notes: Her hymn explores the limits of divine erotic power.

description_brief: Goddess of hunting and wild places, often paired with Apollo.
notes: Marks the boundary between wilderness, purity, and violence.

description_brief: God of wine, ecstatic worship, and disruptive divine epiphany.
notes: His hymn shows divine power arriving through disguise and transformation.

description_brief: Mother of Apollo and Artemis, seeking a place to give birth in the Hymn to Apollo.
notes: Her wandering frames Delos and Delphi as sacred places of arrival.

description_brief: Hearth goddess invoked as the stable center of house and sacrifice.
notes: Small but important figure for domestic and ritual order.

description_brief: Commander of the Achaean army whose quarrel with Achilles opens the Iliad.
notes: His authority is powerful but morally unstable.

description_brief: Aged king of Troy who begs Achilles for Hector's body.
notes: His supplication turns enemy grief into shared human recognition.

description_brief: Achilles' closest companion, whose death brings Achilles back to battle.
notes: The emotional hinge of the Iliad's second half.

description_brief: God of war's destructive force, active in the Iliad among the fighting gods.
notes: Embodies war as appetite and violence rather than strategy.

description_brief: Sea god who opposes Odysseus and intervenes in Trojan War traditions.
notes: A major force of maritime danger and divine anger.

description_brief: Loyal swineherd who shelters the disguised Odysseus and helps restore the household.
notes: Makes humble hospitality central to heroic homecoming.

description_brief: Nymph who keeps Odysseus on Ogygia and offers him immortality.
notes: Her episode tests the value of homecoming against divine pleasure.

description_brief: Leading suitor who abuses Odysseus' household and is first killed in the revenge.
notes: Embodies aristocratic predation inside the home.

description_brief: King of the Phaeacians who hosts Odysseus and sends him home.
notes: His court models idealized hospitality and narrative reception.

description_brief: Roman sky king who oversees fate and divine hierarchy.
notes: In the Aeneid he authorizes Rome's destined future.

description_brief: Roman queen of the gods whose anger opposes Aeneas and repeatedly drives conflict.
notes: Aeneid turns her resistance into part of Rome's eventual order.

description_brief: Mother of Aeneas who protects him and links Roman destiny to divine descent.
notes: Important both erotically and genealogically in Roman myth.

description_brief: Young ally of Aeneas whose death at Turnus' hands demands vengeance.
notes: His death shapes the epic's final moral pressure.

description_brief: King of Latium who receives Aeneas and whose daughter Lavinia is destined for him.
notes: Represents local sovereignty being drawn into Roman origins.

description_brief: Powerful Pandava warrior whose strength and vows drive many acts of vengeance.
notes: Embodies physical force in service of family and dharma.

description_brief: Mother of the Pandavas and Karna, whose choices shape the epic's kinship crisis.
notes: Her secrets make family identity ethically unstable.

description_brief: Blind Kuru king and father of the Kauravas, torn between knowledge and attachment.
notes: A major figure for failed sovereignty and parental partiality.

description_brief: Supreme deity associated with preservation and incarnations including Rama and Krishna.
notes: Links epic heroes to cosmic maintenance.

description_brief: Great god associated with ascetic force, destruction, and divine gifts.
notes: Appears as a source of power and cosmic authority.

description_brief: Hunnish king who marries Kriemhild and hosts the fatal Burgundian visit.
notes: His court becomes the stage for the revenge catastrophe.

description_brief: Burgundian prince and brother of Gunther, Giselher, and Kriemhild.
notes: Part of the doomed royal sibling group.

description_brief: Youngest Burgundian prince, often presented with sympathetic loyalty.
notes: His death intensifies the cost of collective honor.

description_brief: Burgundian/Gjuki king involved in the betrayal of Sigurd and conflict with Atli.
notes: A central node in the heroic oath-and-treasure cycle.

description_brief: King who draws Gudrun's brothers into a fatal conflict over treasure.
notes: Norse heroic memory of Attila turned into kinship tragedy.

description_brief: Goddess associated with desire, seidr magic, wealth, and a share of the battle-slain.
notes: Links erotic, magical, and martial domains.

description_brief: Vanir god associated with fertility, prosperity, and sacral kingship.
notes: Important for Norse abundance and rulership motifs.

description_brief: Volsung hero and father of Sigurd, chosen and tested by Odin.
notes: Links the family saga to divine favor and inherited doom.

description_brief: Brother of Gunnar in the Volsung cycle, caught in the deadly treasure conflict.
notes: A central member of the doomed Gjuki kin group.

description_brief: Smith who fosters Sigurd and urges him to kill Fafnir.
notes: A dangerous mentor whose counsel is bound to cursed wealth.

description_brief: Being transformed into a dragon by greed for cursed treasure and slain by Sigurd.
notes: Both creature and morally legible person in the Volsung cycle.
